Kentucky Property Tax Guide: Appeals, Exemptions and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky

  • Kentucky Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentucky Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Kentucky Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • A taxpayer appealing a PVA real property assessment must first request a conference with the property valuation administrator or deputy, held before or during the inspection period. (KRS 133.120(1)(a) Appeal procedure; source)
  • A taxpayer still aggrieved after the PVA conference may appeal to the county board of assessment appeals by written petition to the county clerk stating reasons, identifying the property and stating the taxpayer's opinion of fair cash value. (KRS 133.120(2)(a)-(b); source)
  • The board of assessment appeals holds a public hearing for each taxpayer appeal and fixes the assessment at fair cash value. (KRS 133.120(3)(a); source)
  • A person aggrieved by the board's decision may appeal to the Board of Tax Appeals under KRS 49.220; a taxpayer who skipped the county board or failed to appear cannot appeal directly to the Board of Tax Appeals. (KRS 133.120; source)
  • Assessment standard is fair cash value; PVAs commonly use sales comparison for homes. All real property is subject to revaluation every year and each parcel must be physically inspected at least once every four years. (The Assessment Process for Real Property | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Kentucky sells certificates of delinquency (tax liens) to third-party purchasers, not the property itself; county clerks run sales from mid-July through late October. (Delinquent Property Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Counties must advertise each sale and list the certificates in the local newspaper and on the clerk's website at least 30 days before the sale. (Delinquent Property Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which Kentucky offices touch a property tax bill from start to finish?

Four local offices each handle one stage of the process. The property valuation administrator (PVA) puts a value on every parcel, the sheriff sends out and takes in the fall bills, the clerk's office inherits whatever stays unpaid, and the county attorney chases those leftovers.

The constitutional yardstick for the PVA is fair cash value, which the Department of Revenue describes as the price a fair voluntary sale would bring. Every parcel must be walked or physically reviewed at least once in four years, and new construction goes on the roll annually. Farm acreage can carry an agricultural value instead. Coal, oil and gas and utility property are valued by the state Office of Property Valuation rather than the PVA.

What is the way to contest a Kentucky assessment?

Begin by asking the PVA or a deputy for a conference. If that conversation leaves you unsatisfied, you file a short written petition at the clerk's office giving your reasons, the parcel you mean and the value you believe is right. Conferences can be held by telephone when you ask.

Public inspection of the roll starts the first Monday in May and lasts 13 days. Your petition must be in by the close of the next workday after the window ends. When a PVA asks and the state agrees, the cutoff can slide by up to 25 days. Bypass the local board, or miss your own hearing, and the later state appeal is off the table.

  • The local board of assessment appeals sits between 25 and 35 days after the roll closes, with a public hearing on each protest.
  • Evidence decides the outcome: sales listings, construction costs, insurance policies, mortgages or loans. A protest with no supporting facts must be denied.
  • Audio recording of the hearing is your right.
  • A paid spokesperson has to fit a role named in the statute, among them lawyer, CPA, tax consultant, licensed broker or appraiser, or be on your payroll, and needs your authorization in writing.

Filing does not pause collection. KRS 133.120(9) has you pay on the figure you claimed in the petition, and if the final value ends up higher you owe the difference plus interest. Bills are sometimes printed before an appeal wraps up, in which case your claimed value is used and a supplemental bill follows for anything the board adds.

Where does a Kentucky owner go after losing at the county board?

The next stop is the state tax appeals board, reached under KRS 49.220. A petition has to arrive inside 30 days of the mailing date on the county board's decision, and the state board rehears the matter from scratch rather than reviewing a record.

The county board owes you a written explanation whenever it changes a value, and it has to inspect the parcel in person on request from you or the PVA. The legislature amended KRS 133.120 effective July 15, 2026, so read the current wording before filing.

What does a typical Kentucky tax year look like on the calendar?

The state's standard schedule is below. Counties that mail after November 1 shift to a version with a 30 day window per stage.

Standard Kentucky real property schedule, as published by the Kentucky Department of Revenue.
DateWhat changes
Jan. 1Valuation snapshot date
Jan. 1 to Mar. 1Owners may list real property
Early May (first Monday)Roll on display for 13 days
Oct. 1 to Nov. 1Early payers save 2%
Nov. 2 to Dec. 31Face amount due
All of January5% added
Feb. 1 to Apr. 1521% added
End of day Apr. 15Unpaid bills leave the sheriff for the clerk

An owner need not re-list land and buildings each year when the prior roll already described them fully and correctly and nothing major has changed.

Who decides the rate that gets multiplied against the assessment?

Every taxing body picks its own rate, but House Bill 44 boxes in the choices. A body can roll its rate back to the compensating level, which keeps income from existing property flat, or choose a rate that lifts that income by no more than 4 percent after a public hearing. Going above the 4 percent line opens the door to a petition and a recall vote. Rates are quoted in cents for each $100 of value.

On the state side, the Department of Revenue announced a 2025 real property rate of 10.6 cents on each $100 of assessed value, down from 10.9 the year before. Assessments were projected to climb 7.54 percent, and the statute limits state revenue growth from existing property to 4 percent. Cities, school districts, counties and special districts stack their own rates on top, so the full rate varies with the parcel's location.

What are the consequences of leaving a Kentucky tax bill unpaid?

Once April 15 passes, the bill converts into a certificate of delinquency that acts as a lien. Charges then pile up by stage.

  • Interest runs 1 percent monthly.
  • A clerk fee of 10 percent and an attorney fee of 20 percent get added, though the attorney's share is forgiven when the owner pays within five business days of the clerk getting the list.
  • Notices go out from the county attorney, the first by May 15 and a second by June 15, along with payment plan offers.
  • Sales to private buyers of the certificates begin in mid-July and may run to late October, with most done by the end of August.

Using a 10 percent penalty, the sheriff's add-on and an assumed 4 percent commission, the department's worked example turns a $1,000 bill into $1,254 once it reaches the clerk. The sample total for a certificate bought by an outside investor in June reaches $1,704.21. What gets sold is the lien. The owner keeps the house but owes the buyer, who tacks on its own fees.

What property tax steps matter when a Kentucky house is being sold?

Learn the balance before the listing goes live. The sheriff can give you the amount on the current bill, and the clerk can say whether a certificate of delinquency sits against the parcel. Counties must post their delinquent lists on a county website and in the newspaper at least 30 days ahead of a sale.

The seller also owes the real estate transfer tax, a charge of $0.50 on every $500 of declared value, which the clerk takes at recording. A foreclosure transfer or a surrender in lieu of foreclosure falls outside it. A homestead exemption on the property should be reported to the PVA at transfer, and organizations with a Section 170 exemption such as churches or libraries use Revenue Form 62A023.

More questions about Kentucky Property Tax Guide

When does a Kentucky property tax bill arrive and when is it due?

Sheriffs mail bills in the fall, with collection starting October 1 or November 1 depending on the county. Payment with a 2 percent discount runs through November 1, and face value is accepted through December 31.

Until what day can I protest my valuation?

The petition is due one workday after the 13 day inspection window ends. That window starts on the first Monday in May, and a PVA conference has to happen before you file.

What penalties hit a late Kentucky bill?

January adds 5 percent, and February 1 through April 15 carries 21 percent. Afterward the bill goes to the clerk, with 1 percent monthly interest and extra fees.

Can the county sell my home over unpaid tax?

What the clerk sells is the lien, in the form of a certificate of delinquency. Your house stays yours, but you then owe the investor who bought the certificate.

Who fixes the state real property rate?

The Department of Revenue sets it each year by July 1 under KRS 132.020. For 2025 it landed at 10.6 cents on each $100 of assessed value.

title: Kentucky Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Kentucky Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Kentucky Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentucky Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Kentucky Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Kentucky House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • To qualify, a person must be at least 65 during the tax period or classified as totally disabled; the application goes to the local PVA no later than December 31 of the eligible tax year. (DOR Sets 2025-2026 Homestead Exemption; source)
  • The applicant must own and maintain the property as a personal residence; only one exemption per residential unit is allowed. (KRS 132.810(2); source)
  • The exemption amount is adjusted every two years if the cost-of-living index has changed by at least 1%. (KRS 132.810; source)
  • When title to exempted property is transferred, the owner, executor, trustee or agent must report the transfer to the PVA; the exemption is tied to the owner, not the property, and a new owner must apply if eligible. (KRS 132.810(3)(h); The Assessment Process for Real Property; source)
  • Disabled applicants under 65 generally reapply annually, except service-connected totally disabled veterans and individuals found totally and permanently disabled under Social Security or other Kentucky statutory rules. (KRS 132.810; source)
Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is the Kentucky homestead exemption?

It is a deduction from the assessed value of a Kentucky home for owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled. Section 170 of the Kentucky Constitution created it, and the Department of Revenue says the deduction is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. Property tax is then figured on whatever value is left.

The Department gives a simple example: a house assessed at a fair cash value of $200,000 is taxed as if it were worth $150,900. The reduction applies to state, county, city and special district taxes alike. In the 2023 tax year the exemption saved more than 474,000 elderly or disabled Kentuckians about $293 million.

Who qualifies for the Kentucky homestead exemption?

Two things have to be true at once: an age or disability test, and a residence test. The statute, KRS 132.810, sets both.

  • The applicant is 65 or older during the year of the application, or was classified as totally disabled on January 1 of that year under a federal agency program or a retirement system inside or outside Kentucky.
  • The applicant owns the property and maintains it as a personal residence.
  • A disabled applicant has received disability payments and keeps the classification for the whole taxation period.
  • Only one exemption is allowed per residential unit, even when two residents both qualify.

Ownership can take several forms. Legal or equitable title, joint tenancy, tenancy in common, a condominium and certain corporate or leasehold interests of more than 98 years all count. A mobile home, an RV classified as real property or a manufactured house qualifies as a residential unit.

How and when do I apply for the exemption?

File with the property valuation administrator, the PVA, in the county where the home sits. The Department of Revenue states that applications are due by December 31 of the eligible tax year and can be submitted online, by mail or in person, depending on what the local PVA office accepts. Phone the office to learn which method it prefers.

An applicant based on age can prove it with a birth certificate, driver's license, passport or other approved document. A disability applicant needs proof of the classification. The state form is titled Application for Exemption Under the Homestead/Disability Amendment.

The valuation you write on the form cannot be used to raise your assessment. If it is, the statute requires an adjustment the next year so that your total tax comes out the same as if the increase never happened.

What if the tax bill is already paid or still unpaid when I qualify?

Timing decides whether you get a reduced bill or a refund. If you qualify before paying the bill for that year, you are entitled to a full or partial exoneration that reflects the exemption. If you qualify after paying, you are entitled to a refund of the tax on the exempt portion of the value.

This matters to heirs and to anyone selling late in the year. A seller who is eligible but never applied can ask the PVA whether an application for the current taxation period is still possible before the December 31 deadline, and can ask the sheriff how the bill would be adjusted.

How does the exemption amount change over time?

The $6,500 written into Section 170 is read as $6,500 in 1972 purchasing power. Every two years, if the federal cost of living index has moved at least 1 percent, the Department of Revenue adjusts the maximum. The 2025 and 2026 figure is $2,750 higher than the 2023 and 2024 figure.

Kentucky homestead exemption amounts. Sources: KRS 132.810 and Kentucky Department of Revenue.
PeriodMaximum exemption
Section 170 original amount (1972 dollars)$6,500
2023 and 2024 assessment years$46,350
2025 and 2026 assessment years$49,100

The department recalculates the amount every second year. Ask your PVA for the figure that applies to the tax year you are working with, since a later biennium will carry a different number.

What happens to the exemption when I sell or inherit the home?

The exemption belongs to the owner, not to the house. When title to an exempt property passes, the owner, administrator, executor, trustee, guardian, conservator or agent has to report the transfer to the PVA. A buyer or an heir who is 65 or disabled has to file a fresh application of their own.

A death also ends the period. If the person holding the classification dies before December 31, the taxation period runs only from January 1 to the date of death. A disabled owner who stops meeting the total disability classification must tell the PVA, and the exemption ends at the close of that taxation period without being prorated.

The exemption has no effect on the deed tax. The grantor still pays fifty cents per $500 of value at recording, unless the transfer falls in one of the listed exceptions such as a foreclosure or a transfer between spouses.

What should a seller with the exemption check before listing?

A few quick checks keep the paperwork clean when a house with an exemption changes hands.

  • Ask the PVA to confirm the exemption is on file for the current year and which person it is tied to.
  • Ask the sheriff for the current bill so you can see whether the exempt value was already applied.
  • Tell the PVA about the transfer once the deed is recorded, since the statute requires the owner or the estate's representative to report it.
  • If the owner has died, keep the date of death handy, because it caps the taxation period for that year.

The buyer should be told the deduction will not carry over automatically. A younger buyer will simply see a bill computed on the full assessment.

Do disabled owners under 65 have to reapply every year?

Usually yes. A totally disabled owner under 65 must apply annually. Two groups are excused after documenting the disability at the first application: service-connected totally disabled veterans of the Armed Forces, and people found totally and permanently disabled under Social Security rules, Kentucky Retirement Systems rules or another provision of the Kentucky Revised Statutes.

Missing an annual renewal can cost a year of savings, so mark December 31 on the calendar if you are in this group.

Is there a second kind of Kentucky homestead protection?

Yes, a separate one that protects against creditors. KRS 427.060 exempts an individual debtor's interest of up to $5,000 in the home the debtor or a dependent uses as a permanent residence, or in a burial plot, from sale under execution, attachment or judgment. It does not apply to foreclose a mortgage given by the owner or for purchase money, and it does not reach debts that existed before the property was bought or improved.

That $5,000 figure is far lower than the tax exemption, and the two are unrelated. The tax deduction lowers a bill; the creditor protection limits what a judgment creditor can take.

Which other property can be exempt under Section 170?

The same section lets Kentucky exempt property held by government, institutions of education, religious institutions, public libraries, cemeteries not run for private profit and institutions of purely public charity. Those owners file Revenue Form 62A023 with the PVA, who may forward unclear cases to the department. The homestead deduction for seniors and disabled owners is a different benefit with its own form.

More questions about Kentucky Homestead Exemption

How much is the Kentucky homestead exemption?

It is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. That amount comes off the assessed value of the home, and tax is figured on the rest.

What age do I have to be to claim it?

You must be 65 or older during the year you apply, or be classified as totally disabled. You also have to own the home and use it as your personal residence.

Where do I file the application?

File with the property valuation administrator in the county where the home is located. The Department of Revenue says applications are due by December 31 of the tax year.

Does the exemption transfer to the person who buys my house?

No. It follows the owner. You must report the transfer to the PVA, and a buyer or heir who is 65 or disabled needs to apply on their own.

Can I get money back if I qualified after paying my taxes?

Yes. KRS 132.810 entitles an applicant who qualifies after the bill is paid to a refund of the tax tied to the exempt value.

title: Kentucky Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Kentucky Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Kentucky Estate and Inheritance Tax: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentucky Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Kentucky Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Kentucky House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • There is no Kentucky estate tax; Kentucky has an inheritance tax on the beneficiary's right to receive property. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Class A beneficiaries (surviving spouse, parent, child, grandchild, sibling and, under the 2026 amendment, nieces and nephews) are exempt from inheritance tax; the 2026 amendment applies to decedents dying on or after January 1, 2026. (KRS 140.070 (2026 Ky. Acts ch. 198); source)
  • Class B (e.g., daughter-in-law, son-in-law, aunt, uncle, great-grandchild) is taxed at 4% to 16%; Class C (all others) at 6% to 16%. (KRS 140.070; source)
  • Class B beneficiaries get a $1,000 exemption and Class C a $500 exemption. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • A return is due within 18 months of death; a 5% discount applies if paid within nine months, and tax over $5,000 may be paid in 10 annual installments. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • If all taxable assets pass to exempt beneficiaries and no federal Form 706 is required, an Affidavit of Exemption suffices for closing the estate. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Kentucky have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

Kentucky has an inheritance tax and no estate tax. The Department of Revenue says the inheritance tax falls on a beneficiary's right to receive property from a deceased person, and the amount depends on the beneficiary's relationship to the decedent and the value received.

Closer relatives get larger exemptions and lower rates. All property of a Kentucky resident is subject to the tax except real estate located in another state, and real estate and personal property in Kentucky owned by a nonresident can also be taxed. That second rule matters when an out-of-state owner leaves a Kentucky house to heirs.

Which heirs owe Kentucky inheritance tax, and at what rates?

Only Class B and Class C beneficiaries owe tax, and the rates run up to 16 percent. KRS 140.070 sorts every recipient into one of three classes.

Kentucky beneficiary classes under KRS 140.070 and KRS 140.080
ClassWho is in itRate rangeExemption
ASurviving spouse, parent, child by blood, stepchild, adopted child, grandchild through those children, nephew, niece, brother, sisterNo taxTotal inheritable interest
BSon-in-law, daughter-in-law, aunt, uncle, qualifying great-grandchild4 percent to 16 percent$1,000
CAny other person, plus institutions such as religious or educational bodies6 percent to 16 percent$500

The current statute text places nieces and nephews inside Class A. The 2026 amendments to KRS 140.070 and 140.080 apply to estates of people who died on or after January 1, 2026.

How are the Class B and Class C brackets built?

The tax is progressive within each class, so only the slice of value inside a bracket takes that bracket's rate. Class B starts at 4 percent on the first $10,000 and rises through 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14 percent to 16 percent on value above $200,000. Class C starts at 6 percent on the first $10,000 and reaches 16 percent on value above $60,000.

Worked from those brackets, a Class B heir who receives $60,000 owes $4,200 before the exemption. The $1,000 exemption comes off the lowest bracket, which trims about $40 and leaves roughly $4,160. A Class C heir receiving the same $60,000 owes $6,300 before the $500 exemption, because the Class C rates start two points higher and climb faster.

  • Exemptions are charged against the lowest brackets first.
  • A surviving spouse's interest can include a qualifying trust or life estate if the personal representative makes the election on the Department of Revenue form by the return due date.
  • For a nonresident decedent, the exemption is prorated by the share of property Kentucky can tax.

When is the Kentucky return due and the tax payable?

For a death on or after July 1, 2026, the return and the payment are due within 24 months of death. A five percent discount applies if the tax is paid within 14 months, and no interest runs if payment arrives inside the 24 months.

  • Deaths before July 1, 2026: 18 months to file and pay, with the five percent discount for payment inside 9 months.
  • Deaths on or after July 1, 2026: 24 months to file and pay, with the five percent discount for payment inside 14 months.
  • After the deadline, interest runs at the tax interest rate defined in KRS 131.010 until the Department of Revenue is paid.
  • If the tax is not paid by the deadline, the personal representative or trustee must give bond for the tax and interest.

A return is required when a federal estate tax return is required and the estate has property Kentucky can reach, and also when any asset passes to a beneficiary taxable under KRS 140.070. The personal representative computes the tax, or the beneficiaries do if no representative serves.

Can an heir pay the tax in installments?

Yes. When a beneficiary's net tax is more than $5,000, the beneficiary may elect to pay in 10 equal annual installments. The first installment is due with the return and the rest follow one year apart.

The election must be written, signed by the beneficiary and filed with the Department of Revenue when the estate return is filed. Interest on the deferred portion starts 24 months after death for a death on or after July 1, 2026, and 18 months after death for earlier deaths. The beneficiary who elects to defer stays personally liable for the unpaid balance.

What changed in Kentucky inheritance tax for deaths in 2026?

Two sets of amendments took effect in the spring of 2026, and each has its own start rule. They change the class list and the clock, so an old guide may give the wrong answer for a recent death.

  • KRS 140.070 and 140.080 were amended effective April 27, 2026, and apply to estates of people who died on or after January 1, 2026.
  • KRS 140.160, 140.210 and 140.222 were amended effective April 14, 2026, and set the 24-month and 14-month periods for deaths on or after July 1, 2026.
  • For a death before July 1, 2026, the 18-month return and payment date and the 9-month discount period still govern.

Pin down the exact date of death before you plan the sale. A death on June 30 and a death on July 1 of the same year sit under different clocks.

How does the tax affect selling an inherited Kentucky house?

Heirs who owe the tax often sell the house to fund it, so the filing deadline should drive the listing date. A Class A heir owes nothing, which leaves the sale timing to probate and the heirs' own plans. A Class B or Class C heir should work out the bill early because the 14-month discount for a death on or after July 1, 2026 can save five percent of the tax.

Before closing, ask the Kentucky Department of Revenue's inheritance tax staff whether the file shows any open balance or lien on the property, and ask the title company what it needs from the estate. Keep the personal representative's letters, the date-of-death value support and the deed handy, since the buyer's title agent will ask for them.

  • List the heirs and note each one's class from KRS 140.070.
  • Estimate the tax for every Class B or C heir using the brackets above.
  • Decide whether proceeds will pay the tax at closing or after distribution.

How long can Kentucky collect inheritance tax?

The Department of Revenue generally has ten years from when the cause of action first accrued to sue to collect. That clock is suspended when an estate is delayed by litigation or another unavoidable cause, and it is suspended during any deferred payment period an heir has elected.

A fraudulent return has no time limit, because the tax can be assessed and collected at any time. Heirs who sell early and distribute everything should keep tax records for the full ten years, since the personal representative and, in a deferral, the beneficiary may be asked about unpaid amounts.

More questions about Kentucky Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Kentucky have an estate tax?

No. The Department of Revenue states there is no Kentucky estate tax. Kentucky taxes the heir's right to receive property instead, through the inheritance tax in KRS Chapter 140.

Does a child or spouse owe Kentucky inheritance tax on an inherited house?

No. A surviving spouse, child, parent, grandchild, sibling, niece and nephew fall in Class A, and Class A beneficiaries are exempt on their total inheritable interest.

How long do heirs have to pay Kentucky inheritance tax after a 2026 death?

For a death on or after July 1, 2026, the tax is payable within 24 months, with a five percent discount if paid within 14 months. Earlier deaths keep the 18-month and 9-month periods.

Can the inheritance tax be paid over time?

Yes, when a beneficiary's net tax exceeds $5,000 the beneficiary can elect 10 equal annual installments. The election is filed in writing with the return, and the first installment is due then.

Does Kentucky tax a Kentucky house owned by someone who lived elsewhere?

Yes. The Department of Revenue says real estate and personal property located in Kentucky and owned by a nonresident can be taxed, and the exemption is prorated for a nonresident decedent.

content:
Kentucky Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Kentucky Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentucky Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House sale
  • Turn the Kentucky Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Kentucky House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Eviction is by forcible detainer complaint to District Court; the warrant issues to the sheriff and trial is by the court unless a party demands a jury. (KRS 383.210; source)
  • A landlord may not retake possession by self-help or by interrupting essential services. (KRS 383.690; source)
Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How does an eviction work in a Kentucky court?

Kentucky calls an eviction lawsuit a forcible detainer action, and it starts in District Court in the county that holds the rental. KRS 383.200 counts a tenant's refusal to hand back possession after the term ends as a forcible detainer, and under KRS 383.210 the court answers a landlord's complaint with a warrant to the sheriff or a constable.

Self-help is off the table. The case moves through the court from filing to the order that returns the house to the owner, and changing locks or cutting services on the way runs into KRS 383.690.

What are the steps from the complaint to getting the house back?

The statutes set the order of events. Several steps carry short deadlines, so a landlord with the paperwork ready before filing saves weeks.

Forcible detainer steps in KRS 383.200 to 383.285
StepWhat happensStatute
ComplaintLandlord files in District Court and a warrant goes to the sheriff or a constableKRS 383.210
ServiceEach defendant gets notice of the time and place at least three days ahead; without notice, no inquiry proceeds against that defendantKRS 383.210, 383.215
TrialThe court tries the case unless a party demands a juryKRS 383.210(2)
JudgmentRestitution of the premises and costs for the landlord, or costs for the defendantsKRS 383.240
Appeal windowSeven days after the findingKRS 383.255
Warrant of restitutionIf no appeal is filed by the seventh day, the court issues the warrant on requestKRS 383.245

How long can a party wait to appeal, and what must be deposited?

Whoever loses can appeal within seven days after the finding. An appellant has to place the rent owed since the case began, plus every later month's rent as it falls due, with the circuit court clerk.

The money stays with the clerk until the court orders it paid out when the appeal ends. Making that deposit perfects the appeal, which pauses the inquisition and sends the file up to circuit court within ten days. An appellant who drops the appeal, along with any surety, answers under KRS 383.260 for the landlord's losses from the delay and the reasonable cost of defending the appeal.

What should each side prepare for the hearing?

Bring paper that proves the tenancy and the default. A landlord's file should hold the lease, the rent ledger, any termination notice with proof of delivery, and photographs if damage is claimed. A tenant's file should hold rent receipts, repair requests and any written agreement about late payments.

  • Either party can ask the court to issue subpoenas for witnesses, and the court can compel attendance under KRS 383.230.
  • A defendant served less than three days before the hearing can move to adjourn until the three days have run, under KRS 383.215.
  • A jury is used only if a party demands one, and the sheriff does not summon one unless a party gives written notice of the demand.

What if the occupant was never a tenant?

KRS 383.290, enacted in 2025, lets an owner ask a law enforcement officer to remove a person who is in the house without permission, but only when every condition fits. A current or former tenant, or anyone who once had the owner's agreement to live there, cannot be removed this way.

  • The person has never been a tenant and never held a written or oral agreement from the owner.
  • The building was closed to the public on the day the person came in.
  • The owner has told the person to go.
  • The person is outside the statute's list of close relatives, and no lawsuit over the property is pending between the two sides.

The owner hands the officer a signed petition, the officer checks identification and serves a notice to vacate, and a sheriff or constable may charge a $20 service fee. Someone wrongfully removed has 60 days to sue in District Court and can win lawyer fees, so reserve this route for clear cases.

What speeds up a Kentucky eviction case, and what is off limits?

Prompt filing, service on every named occupant and complete records move a case fastest. Pulling doors, changing locks or shutting off utilities does the opposite, because KRS 383.690 bars taking possession that way.

  • Think before taking rent once a termination notice is out. KRS 383.675 treats acceptance with knowledge of a default as a waiver of that breach.
  • Avoid rent hikes or threats right after a tenant's code complaint. KRS 383.705 presumes retaliation when the complaint came within the year before.
  • After termination, KRS 383.685 allows a claim for possession and rent plus a separate claim for actual damages and attorney's fees under KRS 383.660(3).

How long can a landlord wait before filing a Kentucky eviction case?

KRS 383.285 bars an inquisition of forcible entry or detainer more than two years after the entry or detainer complained of. That is the outer limit, and the practical window is far shorter.

Where the URLTA has not been adopted, KRS 383.160 lets a landlord retake a house without demand or notice if the case begins within 90 days after a term of a year or longer ends, or within 30 days after a shorter term ends. Miss those windows and the next chance comes later, so file soon after a lease runs out.

What costs and damages can a landlord recover?

The judgment for the landlord restores possession and awards the costs of the case. KRS 383.240 states the form: restitution of the premises plus costs expended, or costs for the defendants if they prevail.

Money claims are separate. After a termination under the URLTA, KRS 383.685 allows a claim for possession and rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach and reasonable attorney's fees. A tenant's willful noncompliance can support actual damages and attorney's fees under KRS 383.660(3). Keep rent ledgers, repair invoices and photographs so those amounts can be proved at trial.

How does a pending eviction affect selling the house?

A pending case does not block a closing, but it decides who has to deliver the keys. Judgment alone does not empty the house, because possession arrives with the warrant of restitution.

Buyers and lenders often want a vacant house, so the contract should name who finishes the case, who pays its costs and what happens if the tenant appeals and the deposit sits with the clerk. Ask the closing attorney how the seller's duties to the tenant are handled once title passes.

  • Get the case number, judgment and any warrant of restitution into the sale file.
  • Confirm whether any rent is sitting with the circuit court clerk after an appeal.
  • Ask the title company whether the occupancy affects the closing date.

Where can a Kentucky landlord find court forms and help?

Call the clerk's office at the District Court for the house's county and ask for the current forcible detainer forms and filing fee. The Kentucky Court of Justice also runs a Legal Self-Help section on its website.

A real estate attorney can confirm which notice rules apply in your city and how a pending case should be handled in the sale contract. Ask the clerk, too, how the court wants service on each occupant arranged with the sheriff's office.

More questions about Kentucky Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Which court handles evictions in Kentucky?

The District Court for the county where the rental stands. The landlord files a forcible detainer complaint, and a warrant then goes to the sheriff or a constable under KRS 383.210.

What is the deadline to appeal a Kentucky eviction judgment?

Seven days after the court's finding. The party who appeals must also deposit the unpaid rent and each later month's rent with the circuit court clerk.

Can an owner change the locks or shut off power to remove a tenant?

No. KRS 383.690 forbids regaining the dwelling by cutting heat, electricity, water, gas or another essential service. The court order is the only route.

Does a sheriff remove a tenant after the judgment?

Yes. If no appeal is filed by the seventh day, the court issues a warrant of restitution on request, which directs the sheriff or constable to put the landlord in possession.

Can I use the quick removal process for a former tenant?

No. KRS 383.290 excludes current and former tenants and anyone who once had the owner's agreement to live there. Those disputes go through forcible detainer.

content:
Kentucky Quitclaim Deed: Recording, Fees and When It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentucky Quitclaim Deed sale
  • Turn the Kentucky Quitclaim Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • For a gift or nominal-consideration deed, the county clerk computes tax on the estimated open-market price unless an exemption applies. (Transfer Tax | Fayette County Clerk; source)
  • County clerk fees are set by KRS 64.012: a $33 fee applies to listed items of up to five pages ($3 per additional page), of which $27 stays with the clerk and $6 goes to the affordable housing trust fund. (KRS 64.012; source)
Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What does a Kentucky quitclaim deed actually transfer?

A quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer holds in a parcel and promises nothing about how good that interest is. The McCracken County Clerk describes it as a deed that operates by way of release, passing any title or claim the grantor may have without a warranty or covenants for title. Kentucky law gives warranty deeds their own wording: KRS 382.030 turns the words with general warranty into a promise to defend the property against all persons, and KRS 382.040 limits that promise to claims made by or through the grantor.

A quitclaim deed carries neither promise. That is why it shows up between relatives, former spouses, co-heirs and people tidying up an old record, and why a buyer paying real money usually wants more than a quitclaim in the chain. Anyone who expects to resell afterward should mention the quitclaim to the closing agent early, so the title search can allow for it.

  • It conveys the grantor's interest, large or small, as it stands on the day of signing.
  • It does not create ownership the grantor never had.
  • It does not remove a mortgage, a judgment lien or an unpaid tax lien from the parcel.

What must a Kentucky deed contain before the county clerk will record it?

KRS 382.135(1) lists what every deed to real property must carry, and a quitclaim deed is a deed for this purpose. The clerk may not lodge a deed that falls short of the list, so a missing line means a rejected filing and a second trip to the courthouse.

  • The full name and the mailing address of the grantor and of the grantee.
  • A statement of the full consideration.
  • An in-care-of address where the tax bill for the transfer year can be sent.
  • A sworn, notarized certificate signed by both sides, either confirming the consideration or stating that the transfer is a gift and giving the estimated fair cash value.

Two more statutes add to the list. KRS 382.335 requires a signed statement on the deed naming the person who prepared it, along with that person's address, and it requires the grantee's mailing address. KRS 382.110 requires the deed to refer to the source of the grantor's title, by book and page when the title came from a recorded deed, or by a plain account of how and from whom the title arrived when it came by inheritance. KRS 382.130 lets a deed made in Kentucky go to record on the maker's acknowledgment before the clerk or before a notary.

Where is a quitclaim deed recorded, and what does recording cost?

Take it to the clerk's office in the county that holds the land, or the county with the larger share if a parcel straddles a line. KRS 382.110(1) sets that rule, and the 2026 General Assembly amended it effective July 15, 2026. The same date brought amendments to KRS 64.012, the fee schedule, which still lists $33 as the base charge for a deed of up to five pages.

Kentucky deed charges named in KRS 64.012 and KRS 142.050
ItemAmount
Recording and indexing a deed, up to 5 pages$33, of which $27 stays with the clerk and $6 goes to the affordable housing trust fund
Each page after the fifth$3
Each added reference to the same instrument$4
Permanent records storage reimbursement$10 under KRS 64.012(3)(a)
Real estate transfer tax, charged to the grantor$0.50 for each $500 of value or fraction of $500

Counties post their own totals. McCracken County's clerk publishes a $50 deed filing fee with the same $3 charge for pages past five. Phone the clerk where your parcel sits and get the all-in figure before the trip.

When does the Kentucky transfer tax apply to a quitclaim deed?

KRS 142.050 puts the tax on the grantor, and the clerk collects it before accepting the deed. When property is sold, it is figured on the full consideration, including any lien. When property is given away, or the deed shows a token price, the statute substitutes the estimated open-market value. The clerk does the arithmetic, which is why a deed that understates the price draws questions.

Subsection (7) lists the exempt transfers. Those most likely to involve a quitclaim deed:

  • Parent to child, or grandparent to grandchild, for a token price only.
  • One spouse to the other, or between former spouses in a divorce.
  • A deed that only confirms or fixes an earlier recorded deed.
  • A transfer whose sole purpose is to secure or release a debt.
  • Partition, foreclosure, or a voluntary surrender in lieu of foreclosure.
  • A trustee to a successor trustee, and certain moves into a trust whose only beneficiary is the grantor.

An exemption does not waive the filing rules. A gift deed from mother to daughter still needs the notarized fair cash value certificate under KRS 382.135 even though no tax is owed.

What if the grantor inherited the property?

A deed from someone who took title by descent has an extra step. Under KRS 382.120 the grantor, any heir at law, or two Kentucky residents with personal knowledge must hand the clerk an affidavit before the deed is filed. The affidavit names the person who died, gives the date of death, says whether that person was married, states where they lived, confirms they died without a will, and lists each heir with age, address, relationship and share.

The clerk records the affidavit and indexes it under the ancestor as grantor and each heir as grantee, charging the same fees as a deed. KRS 382.135(4) adds a duty for estates that pass by will or intestacy: before closing the estate, the personal representative files an affidavit in each county where the land lies, listing who receives each parcel and its estimated value. Heirs who sign quitclaim deeds to one another to consolidate a family house should confirm both affidavits are on file, since the clerk will not take the deed first.

What are the penalties for a false statement on a deed?

KRS 382.990 attaches criminal penalties to the paperwork. A person who willfully and fraudulently gives a false statement of the full actual consideration, or of the full estimated value, under KRS 382.135 commits a Class D felony. A person who knowingly swears to a false statement in the descent affidavit under KRS 382.120 commits a Class A misdemeanor and is liable to anyone injured by its use.

The practical lesson is to write the true figure. If a family member is paying a token amount for a house worth far more, say so on the deed and let the clerk compute the tax on market value or apply the parent and child exemption. Understating the price to save a few dollars of transfer tax creates a recorded document that can be challenged later, and a later buyer's title company will read it.

Does a quitclaim deed help when you plan to sell the house?

It can move the title into the right names so a sale can close, and it can also cause delay. A quitclaim deed leaves every lien and tax debt in place. KRS 382.070 also warns that a seller who leaves part of the price unpaid has no lien against creditors and purchasers unless the deed states what remains unpaid.

Owners who inherited a Kentucky house, fell behind on payments or hold a property with repair problems often ask whether a quitclaim to a relative will simplify things. Usually the better first step is a payoff request to the lender and the county for any unpaid tax, then a plain conversation with a closing attorney. If you want a direct cash sale of a Kentucky house as it stands, a quitclaim deed signed beforehand does not change what the buyer's title company must clear.

More questions about Kentucky Quitclaim Deed

Do I need a lawyer to record a Kentucky quitclaim deed?

No statute makes you hire one, but KRS 382.335 requires the deed to show the name and address of the person who prepared it, signed by that person. Many people have an attorney or a title company draft the document so the consideration certificate, source of title and legal description are right on the first filing.

Is a notary required on a quitclaim deed in Kentucky?

Yes. The grantor's signature must be acknowledged, and KRS 382.135 requires the consideration or gift certificate to be sworn and notarized by both sides. County clerk offices can notarize for a fee set in KRS 64.012, so ask the clerk before you sign anywhere else.

What will recording a Kentucky quitclaim deed set me back?

State law sets $33 for up to five pages and $3 per extra page, and KRS 64.012 also allows a $10 records reimbursement. Transfer tax is fifty cents per $500 of value unless an exemption fits. McCracken County's clerk posts a $50 deed fee, so confirm the figure with the clerk who will record yours.

Can I quitclaim my house to my child and avoid transfer tax?

A transfer between parent and child for only a token price is exempt under KRS 142.050(7)(l). The deed still needs the sworn certificate that calls it a gift and states the estimated fair cash value.

Which office records a Kentucky quitclaim deed?

The county clerk where the property, or most of it, sits. KRS 382.110 sets that rule, and a deed recorded in the wrong county does not give the notice that protects the grantee against later purchasers and creditors.

content:

Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentucky Transfer on Death Deed sale
  • Turn the Kentucky Transfer on Death Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • As of the KRS database update in August 2026, KRS Chapter 391 lists no sections on transfer on death deeds. (KRS Chapter 391 table of contents; source)
  • 2026 SB 34 would create a Kentucky Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act; its last recorded action was 03/24/26, to House Local Government. (2026 RS SB 34; source)
  • Kentucky court form AOC-830, Petition to Dispense With Administration, cites KRS 391.030, 394.145, 395.455 and 396.095 and applies when estate assets are $30,000 or less. (AOC-830 Petition to Dispense With Administration; source)
  • Real estate of a person dying without a will descends under KRS Chapter 391; the DOR notes that survivorship property passes to the surviving co-owner on the deed and not by will or intestacy. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Kentucky Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Kentucky rules with an attorney.

Does Kentucky allow a transfer on death deed?

Not under any statute currently on the books. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, as published through the 2026 Regular Session, list no transfer on death deed sections in KRS Chapter 391, the chapter on descent and distribution. Lawmakers have taken up the idea more than once, but the bills stalled before reaching the governor.

In 2024, House Bill 50 proposed a Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act. Its last recorded action was on January 25, 2024, when it was recommitted to the House Appropriations and Revenue Committee. In 2026, Senate Bill 34 proposed a similar act, and its last recorded action was on March 24, 2026, when it went to the House Local Government Committee. Neither bill produced a law, so an owner who records something labeled a transfer on death deed in Kentucky is relying on a form the statutes do not provide for.

Because the legislature may revisit the subject, check the Legislative Research Commission bill pages before relying on anything you read, including this page.

What would Senate Bill 34 have changed?

The bill summary on the General Assembly's site shows what a Kentucky version would look like. It is useful as a preview and as a warning that the rules would have come with strings attached.

  • A transfer on death deed would not be a lifetime transfer. Ownership would pass at the transferor's death, and the transferor could revoke the deed at any time.
  • The deed would be nontestamentary, meaning it would not need to meet the formalities of a will.
  • It would need to be recorded before the transferor's death, and a floor amendment would have made a deed that was not filed in time void.
  • Any later deed transferring an interest in the same property would revoke the earlier transfer on death deed.
  • The Department of Revenue would supply the forms, the state Medicaid agency would supply a form about any Medicaid lien, and KRS 64.012 would be amended to set a recording fee.
  • The same bill would have created a beneficiary designation for motor vehicle titles.

None of that is law. It is a record of what was proposed, and the amendments show the details were still moving when the bill stopped.

How does Kentucky real estate pass when the owner dies without a will?

KRS 391.010 sets the order of inheritance, and the statute was amended by 2026 Acts chapter 134, effective July 15, 2026. The surviving spouse comes first. Children and their descendants come next, then the parents, then siblings, then grandparents, then aunts, uncles and stepchildren. If no kindred exist, the property vests in the state under KRS 393.020.

Surviving spouse's share of intestate real estate under KRS 391.010(1)(a)
Who survives the ownerSpouse's share
No descendantsThe entirety
Descendants, all of them also descendants of the spouseThe entirety
Descendants who are not lineal descendants of the spouseOne-half
Shared descendants, plus a spouse with other descendants of their ownOne-half

Whatever does not go to the spouse passes to the next group in the order above. A family that wants a different result for a specific house needs a will, a trust or a lifetime deed, because a deed to take effect at death does not exist as a statutory tool.

What can an owner do instead of a transfer on death deed?

Kentucky owners use the tools the statutes do recognize. None of them is a perfect substitute, and each carries tradeoffs worth discussing with an estate attorney before signing.

  • A will. It passes the house to the person you name, but the estate usually goes through probate before the deed can be signed.
  • A deed with survivorship wording. KRS 381.120 says a joint tenant's share goes to that person's heirs or devisees, so survivorship has to be expressed in the instrument. KRS 381.130(1) carves out an estate conveyed to persons when it manifestly appears from the instrument that the share of the one who dies should belong to the others.
  • A lifetime deed, with or without a retained life estate. It moves title now, so recording costs and the new owner's rights begin today.
  • A trust. KRS 142.050(8) exempts certain transfers to and from a trustee from the transfer tax, including a transfer where the grantor is the sole beneficiary.

KRS 391.360 treats written provisions for a nonprobate transfer in instruments such as a trust, a conveyance or a deed of gift as nontestamentary, and it leaves creditors' rights untouched. Whether a particular document achieves what its signer hopes is a question for an attorney, not for a printed form.

Can joint owners change the way a Kentucky survivorship deed works?

A joint tenant can partition their share during life. KRS 381.130(2) says one or more joint tenants of real property may partition their interest by deed or other instrument that states the intent to partition and is recorded with the county clerk where the land lies. The partition takes effect when the instrument is recorded, and it converts the partitioning tenant's interest into a tenancy in common.

One exception protects couples. Residential property owned exclusively by a husband and wife as joint tenants with right of survivorship, and actually occupied by them as a principal residence, cannot be partitioned this way. For everyone else, a survivorship deed is only as stable as the co-owners' willingness to leave it alone, so a parent who adds a child to a deed to avoid probate also hands that child a present interest in the house.

What must heirs file before a Kentucky inherited house can be sold?

Two affidavits come up repeatedly. KRS 382.135(4) requires the personal representative of an estate that passes by will or intestacy to file an affidavit with the county clerk of each county where property lies, naming each recipient with an address and giving the full or fair market value used for estate purposes. KRS 382.120 requires an affidavit of descent before a deed from an heir is filed, setting out the ancestor's name, date of death, marital status, residence, the fact of intestacy and each heir's relationship and share.

After those are in order, the deed itself must follow KRS 382.135(1) and KRS 382.335: full names and mailing addresses, a statement of consideration, an in-care-of address for the tax bill, the notarized certificate, the signed preparer statement and a reference to the source of title. For a house passing from an estate, the source statement describes how and from whom the heirs obtained it.

Will a deed that passes at death avoid Kentucky transfer tax or recording fees?

A lifetime deed to a family member is a deed like any other. KRS 142.050(7)(l) exempts a transfer between parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, made for only nominal consideration, and a gift deed still requires the notarized certificate stating the estimated fair cash value. The clerk's fee under KRS 64.012 is $33 for up to five pages, plus $3 for each page after that.

Before recording any deed in a parent's name, confirm with the county clerk what that office will accept, and with a qualified attorney how the transfer affects the owner's own security. A deed that gives up control during life is a bigger step than a document that would take effect only at death.

More questions about Kentucky Transfer on Death Deed

Can I record a transfer on death deed in Kentucky?

No statute authorizes one. KRS Chapter 391 contains no transfer on death deed sections through the 2026 session, and the 2024 and 2026 bills proposing one did not become law. Ask an estate attorney which authorized instrument fits your goal.

What happens to my house in Kentucky if I die without a will?

It descends under KRS 391.010. A surviving spouse takes the entire real estate when the decedent had no descendants or when all descendants are shared with the spouse, and one-half when some descendants are not the spouse's. The rest follows the statutory order of kin.

Is joint ownership with a child a safe way to avoid probate?

It carries risk. Survivorship must appear in the deed, a joint tenant can partition their share by recorded deed under KRS 381.130, and the child becomes a present co-owner during your life. Speak with an attorney first.

Will Kentucky pass a transfer on death deed law soon?

Nothing in the statutes says so. Senate Bill 34 of 2026 last moved on March 24, 2026, when it went to the House Local Government Committee, and House Bill 50 of 2024 stalled in January 2024. Bill status is public on the legislature's website.

Can heirs sell an inherited Kentucky house quickly?

Yes, once the estate paperwork is in place. The personal representative's affidavit under KRS 382.135(4) and any affidavit of descent under KRS 382.120 must be filed with the county clerk, and the deed has to meet the content rules before it will be recorded.

content:

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Kentucky's individual income tax is based on the Internal Revenue Code in effect as of December 31, 2024; the page states a four percent rate. (Individual Income Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Kentucky tax house sale profit apart from other income?

No. Kentucky has no capital gains schedule. KRS 141.020 levies one flat percentage on the entire net income of a resident, so profit from a Kentucky closing simply joins the rest of that year's income.

Because the state rate is flat, the real swing factor for a Kentucky seller is how much profit survives the federal rules first. A homeowner of long standing may shield nearly all of it. A landlord, a flipper or an heir who sells an inherited house usually cannot. Ask the Kentucky Department of Revenue how an excluded gain is carried onto Form 740 before you file.

Which Kentucky rate applies to a closing in 2026 or later?

A closing in a taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2026 is taxed at 3.5 percent of net income. The rate has stepped down several times, so the year of the closing matters.

Kentucky individual income tax rate by taxable year, from KRS 141.020(2)
Taxable years beginningRate on net income
2018 through 20225 percent
20234.5 percent
2024 and 20254 percent
2026 and after3.5 percent

Further cuts for 2027 and later years depend on budget triggers and a vote of the General Assembly, and the statute says the department cannot lower the rate by itself. As a sketch, a $40,000 taxable profit costs about $1,400 at 3.5 percent and would have cost $1,600 at 4 percent.

How much profit can a Kentucky homeowner shield under the federal main-home rule?

Federal law lets a seller shield up to $250,000 of profit on a main home, or $500,000 on a joint return. The IRS attaches two tests, and both are measured over the five years that end on the closing date.

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for two years or more.
  • Use: you lived there as a residence for two years or more. On a joint return, each spouse must meet this test personally.
  • The two-year spans can fall at different points inside the five-year window.
  • A seller who shielded profit on a different home during the two years before this closing generally cannot claim it again.
  • Members of the Uniformed Services, the Foreign Service and the intelligence community on qualified extended duty may freeze the five-year window for as long as a decade.

A Form 1099-S from the closing agent creates a duty to report the sale even if no tax is due. Reporting is also required whenever part of the profit is left over after the shield.

How do I measure the profit on a Kentucky house?

Profit is the net amount you realize at closing minus your adjusted basis. Basis begins with the purchase price plus sales tax and buying costs, rises with improvements that add value, and falls with depreciation claimed and insurance money received for casualty or theft losses.

A homeowner who put a new roof or a finished basement into a Kentucky house should keep those invoices, because each one lifts basis and trims the taxable profit. An heir or a recipient of a gift follows different basis rules, which the IRS explains in Publication 551. A house held for one year or less produces short-term gain, taxed like wages, while a longer hold produces long-term gain.

The IRS also says a loss on a home you lived in cannot be deducted. A sale below basis gives no write-off.

How does the federal government tax the profit left after the shield?

Long-term profit sits in one of three federal tiers, zero, fifteen or twenty percent, chosen by taxable income and filing status. The IRS republishes the income cutoffs each year in Topic no. 409, so read the table for your closing year instead of relying on an old figure.

Depreciation changes the picture for rentals. The slice of profit that reflects depreciation on real property (unrecaptured section 1250 gain) can be taxed at up to 25 percent federally. Reporting runs through Form 8949 and Schedule D.

What changes if the Kentucky house was a rental or came by inheritance?

A house you never lived in fails the use test, so the main-home shield is generally unavailable. Depreciation you took reduces basis and raises profit, and a rental that has run for years can produce a large number even when the market barely moved.

An inherited house raises two separate questions. One is income tax on profit above basis, which follows Publication 551. The other is Kentucky inheritance tax, a levy on the heir's right to receive property under KRS Chapter 140 that is unrelated to your Form 740. Class A heirs, such as a spouse, child or sibling, are exempt from that second tax.

  • Pull depreciation schedules before listing, not after closing.
  • Ask the estate's personal representative for the valuation papers used on the estate return.
  • Choose a closing date with the tax year and its rate in mind.

What if I live outside Kentucky or moved during the year?

A nonresident owes Kentucky tax on income from tangible property in Kentucky, and a house here counts as that property. KRS 141.020 also taxes a part-year resident as a resident for the months of residency and as a nonresident for the remaining months.

The Department of Revenue prints Form 740 and Form 740-NP, and its credit instructions mention both. Ask the department which return fits your move date, because that choice decides whether the whole profit or only the Kentucky-sourced part is reported.

Which Kentucky credits can a big sale affect?

The department's individual income tax page lists a $40 credit for each person aged 65 or over and for a legally blind individual, and a $20 credit for Kentucky National Guard members. It also describes a nonrefundable family size tax credit under KRS 141.066 that is tied to modified gross income and family size, with a 2025 ceiling of $42,760.

A closing can lift modified gross income for the year, so a household that normally qualifies for the family size credit may lose it in a sale year. Run the numbers with the closing profit included before you decide on the sale date.

What paperwork should a Kentucky seller gather before closing?

Collect the records that fix basis and residency now, because the closing agent's Form 1099-S shows only the sale price. A short list saves a preparer hours later.

  • The closing statement from your own purchase, showing cost and buying expenses.
  • Receipts for work that added value, such as a roof, an addition or a finished basement.
  • Depreciation schedules if any part of the house produced rent.
  • Proof of the dates you lived there, such as utility bills and the address on your license.
  • For an inherited house, the estate valuation papers and the personal representative's letters.

The IRS notes that a taxable profit may call for estimated tax payments during the year. Ask the Department of Revenue whether Kentucky estimated payments apply to your sale year, and set aside part of the proceeds.

More questions about Kentucky Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does Kentucky give a break for selling a main home?

The Kentucky rate statute contains no home sale break of its own. The federal shield of $250,000 single or $500,000 joint controls how much profit you have, so confirm with the Department of Revenue how it appears on Form 740.

What rate will Kentucky charge on my profit for a 2026 closing?

The rate is 3.5 percent of net income for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, the same percentage that applies to wages.

Do I report the sale if the whole profit is shielded?

Yes, when you receive a Form 1099-S or when any portion of the profit is left over. Use Form 8949 and Schedule D where they apply.

Can I write off a loss on a house I lived in?

No. The IRS says losses on personal-use property such as a home are not deductible.

Does someone who lives in another state owe Kentucky tax on selling a Kentucky house?

Yes. The statute reaches a nonresident's income from tangible property in Kentucky. Ask the department which return applies and how credits are prorated.
